questions.q: In a cathode ray tube, from which electrode do the cathode rays stream, and what is its charge?
options: From the anode, the positive electrode
From the cathode, the negative electrode
From the glass walls, which carry no charge
From the leftover gas in the middle of the tube
questions.explanation: The rays pour out of the cathode — the negative plate — race down the tube and make the far glass glow green. Goldstein named them 'cathode rays' in 1876 precisely because they originate at the cathode.

questions.q: What did Crookes's Maltese cross experiment demonstrate about cathode rays?
options: That the rays carry negative charge
That the rays travel in straight lines, because the metal cross cast a sharp shadow
That the rays are a form of heat
That the rays can pass straight through solid metal
questions.explanation: A metal Maltese cross placed in the beam threw a crisp dark shadow on the glowing glass, exactly as an opaque object blocks light. A sharp shadow means the rays travel in straight lines.

questions.q: Hertz fired cathode rays between charged plates and saw no deflection. Why did Thomson conclude this was a misleading result rather than proof the rays were uncharged?
options: Hertz had used the wrong sign of charge on his plates
Leftover gas in the tube was ionised, and those ions piled onto the plates and cancelled out the electric field
The rays were moving too fast to feel any electric force
Magnetic fields always cancel electric fields inside a glass tube
questions.explanation: In Hertz's poor vacuum the rays knocked electrons off the residual gas, creating ions that rushed to the plates and short-circuited the field. With no field actually present in the beam region, the rays could not be deflected. Thomson's better vacuum removed the gas, and then the beam bent toward the positive plate.

questions.q: In Thomson's velocity selector, the electric and magnetic forces are balanced so the beam travels straight. What does this configuration let him calculate directly?
options: The charge of each particle on its own
The mass of each particle on its own
The speed of the particles, equal to E divided by B
The radius of the beam's circular path
questions.explanation: When the beam is undeflected the electric force eE equals the magnetic force evB. The charge cancels from both sides, leaving v = E/B — and Thomson had set both E and B himself, so he could read off the speed (tens of thousands of km/s, up to about a third of the speed of light).

questions.q: Thomson's particles had a charge-to-mass ratio about 1800 times that of the hydrogen ion. What independent evidence convinced him this meant a tiny mass rather than a gigantic charge?
options: The particles glowed brighter than any known atom
Lenard's measurements showed the particles travel enormous distances through matter before being stopped, which a heavily charged particle could not do
The particles were always emitted from platinum cathodes
The particles moved at exactly the speed of light
questions.explanation: A particle carrying a huge charge would grab every atom it passed and be stopped almost at once. Lenard's mean-free-path data showed the cathode-ray particles glided through matter as if it were empty space — so they must be extremely small, not extremely charged. The mass on the bottom of the ratio is tiny.

questions.q: How did Thomson establish that his corpuscle was a universal constituent of all matter, not just a fragment of one substance?
options: He calculated it from theory without doing any experiments
He repeated the measurement while changing the gas (air, hydrogen, CO2) and the cathode metal (aluminium, platinum) and got the same charge-to-mass ratio every time
He found the particle only inside hydrogen gas
He showed the particle had the same mass as a hydrogen atom
questions.explanation: If the particles were chips of the gas or the metal, the ratio would shift when he swapped them. It never did — air, hydrogen, CO2, aluminium, platinum all gave the same charge-to-mass ratio. The only conclusion: the same particle is a building block of every kind of matter.

questions.q: From memory: why could Thomson's charge-to-mass experiment give only a ratio, and not the charge or the mass of the particle on its own?
keyPoints: A stronger force bends the beam more, but a heavier particle bends less because of its inertia — mass resisting the force.
The charge sets how strongly the field grips the particle in the first place.
When you do the algebra, charge and mass never separate — they come out welded together as charge divided by mass.
An independent measurement of the charge (later, from Millikan's oil-drop experiment) is needed to prise the mass apart from the ratio.
questions.explanation: If you recalled that bending depends on both how hard the field grips (charge) and how hard the particle is to push (mass), so the two only ever appear as e/m, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: From memory: Crookes's paddle wheel is a famous myth. What actually turns it, and what does it really prove about cathode rays?
keyPoints: It does NOT turn from the momentum of electrons hitting the vanes — Thomson's 1903 calculation showed that force is far too weak (a modern analysis found it over 100x too weak).
It turns by heat: the rays warm the vanes, the warm surface heats the thin gas next to it, and that hot gas expands and pushes harder than the cooler gas on the other side (the radiometer effect).
So the paddle wheel only proves the rays carry energy, not that they carry momentum.
Thomson's real proof that the rays are charged particles came from the field deflections and the charge-to-mass ratio, not the wheel.
questions.explanation: The lesson is that an experiment can give a true conclusion (the rays are particles) for completely the wrong reason. If you got 'heat / radiometer effect, proves energy not momentum', mark it Good or Easy.

questions.q: In Thomson's velocity selector the beam passes undeflected when the electric and magnetic forces balance. Starting from the force balance, show that the particle speed is v = E/B.
questions.given: Electric force on the charge = eE.  Magnetic force on the moving charge = evB.  At balance the beam is undeflected, so the two forces are equal and opposite.
working: Divide both sides by \(e\) (the charge cancels): \(E = vB\)
questions.explanation: Because the charge e appears on both sides it cancels, leaving the speed in terms of two quantities Thomson set himself — the field strengths E and B. This is why the velocity selector measures speed without needing to know the charge.

questions.q: Using the values quoted in the episode — the elementary charge e = 1.6 x 10^-19 C and the electron mass m = 9 x 10^-31 kg — calculate the electron's charge-to-mass ratio e/m.
questions.explanation: Dividing the charge by the mass gives about 1.8 x 10^11 C/kg — roughly 1800 times the charge-to-mass ratio of the hydrogen ion, exactly the 'off the scale' figure Thomson found that proved the corpuscle is far lighter than any atom.
